t: Minimum Cost to Split into Ones — Every Pair Pays Once
o: Splitting x into a+b=x costs a·b, repeated until n ones. Examples give 3→3 and 4→6, which equal C(3,2)=3 and C(4,2)=6. The key observation: each operation separating pieces charges a·b, which is exactly the number of unordered pairs of final units that become separated for the first time. Every pair of the n units is separated exactly once over the whole process, regardless of strategy, so the total is always n(n-1)/2.
k: Cost a·b counts the pairs of ultimate ones split apart by that operation.
Each of the C(n,2) pairs is charged exactly once across the entire process.
Therefore the answer is strategy-independent: n(n-1)/2.

a.i: By the pairing argument, return n*(n-1)//2 directly.

Define cost[x] = min total cost to reduce x to ones. Trying all first splits a + (x-a) gives cost[x] = min a(x-a) + cost[a] + cost[x-a], which evaluates to the same closed form — useful to convince yourself (or an interviewer) the formula is right.
s: For x = 2..n, take min over a in [1, x/2] of a*(x-a) + cost[a] + cost[x-a].
a.t: O(n²) — all first splits for each x

w: Lead with the pairing insight — it turns a seemingly computational problem into O(1). The DP is a nice sanity check and a fallback if you cannot prove the invariant. Edge case: n = 1 costs 0. Follow-up: what if the cost were a+b or a²+b²? (Then the total would depend on strategy and genuine optimization is needed.)
